leading_positions.synthesis: Four of eight members (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Pearce) prefer optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye, as the sole prize part. All four propose the same two laureates and citations built around magic-wavelength trapping and roughly 1e-18 uncertainty. They share the view that the credit is the least contested on the shortlist. They do not share a weighting of risk: Danielsson and Pearce moved to B052 in round 1 from other first choices (B006 and B010) mainly on attribution grounds, while Kroll and Lindroth put it first from the start on physics. The same four name overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and the unfinished redefinition of the second as the main reservations, and Danielsson and Pearce keep a different candidate as an alternative (B006 and B056 for Danielsson; B010 and B043 for Pearce). Four other members list B052 only as an alternative, so it is a first choice for half the committee and a fallback for the other half, with no round-1 objection to the merit of the physics.

Eriksson alone prefers topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), as a new class of matter with a clean theory-plus-experiment structure, and names B052 and B044 as alternatives. Lindroth lists B021 as a fallback and Olsson as an alternative, but both, along with Mehlig, regard the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as a serious weakness, and the 2016 topological-phases prize is raised as a closeness concern. Eriksson would accept B052 if attribution is judged irreparable.

Mehlig alone prefers ultracold-atom quantum simulation in optical lattices with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, valuing conceptual originality and mature confirmation. The same shortlist item attracts an unresolved choice of third name (Zoller versus Esslinger), and Zoller also appears on B009. Mehlig names B052 and B056 as alternatives and says he would be comfortable with B052 if the committee prefers attribution certainty to breadth.

Johansson alone prefers circuit quantum electrodynamics with Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin, arguing for a single well-defined achievement with long independent confirmation. He concedes that Blais versus Girvin cannot be settled on the supplied evidence and that the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize creates an adjacency question. His alternatives are B052 and B009.

Olsson alone prefers spherical-aberration correction in electron microscopy (Rose, Haider, Urban), as a clearly attributable invention overcoming a fundamental optical limit. She acknowledges that no other member prefers it and that the STEM corrector lineage (Krivanek, Dellby) lies outside the three names. Her alternatives are B052 and B021, and she calls B052 the strongest consensus candidate.

areas_of_agreement: All eight members name B052 in their round-1 file, four as the preferred configuration and four as an alternative, and none disputes that the lattice-clock physics is original, reproduced by independent groups and measured at about 1e-18.
All eight preferred configurations are single-part prizes, and every member states that attribution within three names is a decisive criterion in choosing among candidates.
Members who comment on B010 (Danielsson, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce) agree the Higgs discovery is scientifically beyond question, and none expresses support for that trio as the sole prize in round 1.

Members who comment accept that the Katori and Ye credit is the cleanest two-name configuration on the shortlist, and that any citation should tie the award to the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realisation and not to optical clocks in general.

Members who comment on B021 and B056 (Eriksson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Johansson, Kroll) accept those candidates as mature and important and place their objections on credit and prior recognition, not on the physics.
scientific_disputes: Whether the lattice clock is a distinct physical mechanism (magic-wavelength lattice with Lamb-Dicke confinement for parallel interrogation of many atoms) or an incremental advance in a precision-spectroscopy lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012. Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce hold the former; Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson raise the latter as a real concern, and Eriksson would accept B052 without objection if clean credit is preferred.

Whether a conceptually broader candidate should outrank the clocks. Eriksson sets a new class of matter (B021) above a precision invention, and Mehlig sets a qualitatively new class of many-body experiments (B044) above a precision improvement. Kroll counters that the clock tests physics and not only serves as a tool.

Whether instrument and architecture achievements, namely aberration correction (B011), circuit QED (B056) and the clock itself, count as discoveries or inventions in the statutory sense, and how a citation should say what is new in physics terms.
Whether analogue quantum simulation (B044) has already produced a decisive scientific result or is still a maturing method, which only Mehlig addresses directly.
Whether Olsson's claim that B011 fits a measurement-enabling criterion at least as well as B052 holds, which Kroll and Pearce answer by pointing to the clock's direct tests of fundamental physics.
attribution_disputes: B052: Katori and Ye are accepted as the proposer and the record-setting realiser, but Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce all note that PTB, SYRTE, NIST, Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley and Bloom built or improved strontium and ytterbium platforms outside a two-name credit. Several members add that priority details are recalled from memory and unverified.

B010: the proposed trio (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) are founding spokespersons and project leaders, and Danielsson, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce himself observe that they are different from the 2012 analysis leaders. The dispute is whether detector and project leadership can stand for a result obtained by thousands.

B021: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that led to Molenkamp's experiment, and Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy and Hasan were decisive for the 3D generalisation. Eriksson would narrow the citation to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant; Lindroth and Mehlig regard the omission as decisive.

B044: four credited names for three places. In the shortlist's opening proposals Mehlig, Kroll, Lindroth and Johansson named Bloch, Greiner and Zoller; Pearce's opening proposal was Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, and Mehlig accepts that as a weaker fallback. Zoller also appears on B009.

B056: four names for three places, with Girvin and Blais as the contested third (Johansson, Mehlig and Danielsson propose Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin; Johansson and Danielsson suggest tying the citation to the experimental realisation).
B011: the TEM corrector lineage (Rose, Haider, Urban) versus the STEM corrector lineage (Krivanek, Dellby), which a three-name list cannot cover.
maturity_disputes: Whether the prize should wait for the formal redefinition of the second. Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce say the confirmed physics does not depend on an SI decision, while Eriksson and Olsson treat the pending redefinition as a reason to wait or as a timing argument that does not apply to B011, and Mehlig raised it in his opening.

Whether the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes B056 a premature second award to one community. Johansson says it is a separable discovery and a tie-breaker at most, while Kroll and Mehlig treat it as a reason for sequencing.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize makes B021 a continuation rather than a distinct discovery; Eriksson and Olsson say it is distinct, and Lindroth, Mehlig and Johansson are more cautious.

Whether COBE (2006) and Planck (2019) leave a separate WMAP discovery (B006) to be credited; Danielsson, who ranked B006 first in the opening, has moved it to an alternative on this point, and Olsson and Pearce press the same question.
Whether the clock's overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is complementary or incremental depends on citation wording, which Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce each address.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Kroll: a research stay in John Hall's laboratory during his doctoral period, the JILA group in which Jun Ye trained and worked; no co-authorship with Katori or Ye is documented, and he asks whether disclosure or recusal is needed for B052.

Johansson: directs WACQT and works on superconducting circuits and circuit QED, with Chalmers colleagues Delsing and Wilson in the same area; field proximity and a connection to the 2025 prize community on B056, with no specific tie to Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf or Girvin. He asks the chair to consider recusal on B056.

Olsson: works directly with aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy at Chalmers, the technique in B011, and is the only member to prefer it; no tie to Rose, Haider or Urban is recorded. She notes the field proximity could be seen as bias.

Eriksson: works in theoretical magnetism and electronic-structure theory, close to the topological-materials field of B021, which he says may raise his enthusiasm; no tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp is recorded.

Pearce (chair): background in CERN-based particle physics and in cosmic-ray and gamma-ray instruments (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+) is close to the subjects of B010 and B043; no tie to any credited person is recorded and he recuses from none of them. His own preferred prize, B052, carries no flagged conflict.
questions_for_round2: Can the four members who prefer B052 state what, in physical terms, separates the magic-wavelength lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, in a citation that Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson would accept as a distinct discovery rather than an increment?

Should the committee wait for the redefinition of the second, or is the confirmed 1e-18 performance sufficient? Kroll, Lindroth and Danielsson say it is; Eriksson and Olsson treat timing as a live issue, and Mehlig has not yet said whether his seventh place rested on timing alone. Mehlig, what is your remaining objection to B052 beyond overlap and timing?

Do Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson, who list B052 only as an alternative, regard it as acceptable as the sole prize this year, and if not, what specific change in evidence or citation would be needed? Is any of their own preferred candidates (B021, B044, B056, B011) ranked above it on merit if its attribution problems were settled?

Is the two-name credit of Katori and Ye defensible given the contributions of the PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo groups, and could the citation be framed around the lattice scheme and its record demonstrations so that the omission is justified, or does a third name need to be added?

For B021, can a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant be drawn so that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's omission is defensible, and does the 2016 prize preclude it? Eriksson, Lindroth and Mehlig should say whether the HgTe proposal was necessary to the experimental claim.

For B044 and B056, which third name should be credited (Zoller or Esslinger; Girvin or Blais), and does the evidence in the files allow that to be settled? Does the 2025 circuits prize bar B056, and should Johansson recuse on B056 if it stays under consideration?

Does any member, after round 1, still consider the Higgs experimental discovery (B010) or WMAP (B006) a viable sole prize, and if so what attribution would they defend to answer the objections that detector or project leadership does not stand for the 2012 analysis or the COBE and Planck record?
Is there a case for a two-part prize this year, such as B052 with another candidate, and could it fit within the three-person limit? Olsson says it could not without splitting B011's credit.
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 is a four-way split in first preferences with a shared fallback: four of eight members prefer B052 as the sole prize, and each of B021, B044, B056 and B011 is preferred by exactly one member, and all four of those members also naming B052 as an alternative. The disagreements are mainly about attribution limits and timing and not about the quality of the physics, and the main open question for round 2 is whether the objections raised by the minority positions are about the clock itself or about the merits of their own preferred candidates.
